q: What is the first step in building a simulation?
o: decide the question and the number that answers it
why: Without a clear question, such as 'chance of arriving by 8:35', a simulation never ends.

q: The bus comes at any moment in the next 10 minutes, all moments equally likely. Which distribution is that?
why: Uniform: every value in the range is equally likely.

q: Walk 5 minutes, a typical 5-minute wait and a typical 20-minute ride. What total does the 'typical values' guess give?
Why do most simulated commutes take longer than the 30-minute typical guess?
o: the ride can run 10 minutes long but only 5 short, so long trips pull the total up
why: Skewed inputs make the average larger than the most likely value.

o: 80% of trips take 35.3 minutes or less
the trip is late 80% of the time
why: A percentile is the value that the given share of runs come in at or below.

q: An expert gives a minimum, a most likely value and a maximum. A natural distribution is …
why: Triangular and PERT are built from exactly those three numbers.

q: Experts' stated minimum and maximum are usually wide enough.
why: Myth. People anchor on the plan, so stated ranges are usually too narrow; ask for P10 and P90 and widen.

q: On rainy days the bus is late AND the ride is slow, but you simulate them as unrelated. The late tail looks …
why: Bad waits and bad rides then rarely coincide, so very late days are understated.

q: Plan: design 10, then max(build 20, content 12), then test 5 days. What is the planned total?
Past projects finished beyond your P90 in 9 out of 10 cases. What does that tell you?
o: the input ranges are far too narrow
why: A sound P90 is exceeded about 10% of the time; 90% means the inputs understate risk.
